name: The Markdown Editor
tagline: Minimal macOS Markdown editor with live rendering, local files, GitHub sync, and optional AI-tool workflow

verdictSummary: The useful solo loop is very buildable: point a desktop app at an ordinary folder, edit Markdown with a good preview, save safely, and use the repository that is already there. The paid app earns its modest price through restrained Mac-native interaction design, rendering edge cases, reliable file watching, and a GitHub flow that does not make a writer learn Git. Those are execution advantages, not a structural moat.
coreLoopDIY: Open a local folder of Markdown files, edit one with immediate rendered feedback, autosave it in place, and explicitly pull or push the existing Git repository.
replacementScope: personal replacement for the local editing and existing-repository sync loop
requirements: Git installed if repository sync is wanted
whatYouLose: the original's finely tuned single-pane rendered-writing interaction
its tested typography, theme, and image-layout polish
a guided GitHub connection flow that hides Git details
future maintenance and compatibility work by the app's developer
moatNotes: Mac-native editing feel, rendering edge cases, and low-friction Git workflow
whyPeopleStillPay: A Markdown file is not the difficult part. People pay for an editor that gets out of the way, makes long documents look right while they are writing, catches the awkward image and table cases, and turns an existing Git repository into a button rather than an evening. The replacement below is enough for one person's folder; its rough edges are precisely what the paid editor removes.
ongoingBurden: Maintain Tauri and CodeMirror upgrades, Markdown and KaTeX rendering behavior, filesystem race handling, and compatibility with the user's Git configuration.

priorArt.name: CodeMirror
priorArt.desc: Extensible code editor toolkit with a Markdown language package and decoration system.

priorArt.name: Tauri
priorArt.desc: Desktop-app toolkit with a small Rust backend and native filesystem dialogs.

alternatives.name: MiaoYan
alternatives.desc: A local-first Swift Markdown editor with preview, backlinks, LaTeX, history, and a command line; a little more note app, a little less deliberate restraint.

facts.install: Install a macOS app from Homebrew or GitHub Releases; the project also documents an iPhone app and CLI.
facts.dataFormat: Markdown files in a folder chosen by the user; an external cloud-drive client may sync that folder.
facts.gapVsPaid: Its three-column note workflow, backlinks, and cloud-folder conventions are broader than the paid editor's intentionally spare writing surface.

alternatives.name: MarkText
alternatives.desc: WYSIWYG Markdown on all three desktop platforms; it brings more editor than serenity.

facts.install: Download the desktop app for macOS, Windows, or Linux from the project's releases.
facts.dataFormat: Local Markdown documents opened by the desktop editor.
facts.gapVsPaid: It is a capable cross-platform WYSIWYG editor, but does not target the same tightly constrained Mac-native UI or built-in GitHub sync workflow.

alternatives.name: Zettlr
alternatives.desc: A full publication workbench with citations, export pipelines, and search; bring it when a quiet file editor has become a thesis.

facts.install: Download installers for macOS, Windows, or Linux from the project, or use a documented package manager route.
facts.dataFormat: Local documents opened by the desktop app, with export support for publication formats.
facts.gapVsPaid: Zettlr is far more capable for citations and publishing, but its broader workspace is not the paid app's simple, low-control writing surface.

notes: The editor's site explicitly says it is not open source today and promises a 3-day trial after launch day; do not frame the DIY build as an official clone.
prompt:
Build a personal, local-first replacement for The Markdown Editor in an empty folder.
Use exactly Tauri 2, React 19, TypeScript, Vite, CodeMirror 6, unified/remark, rehype-katex, and a Rust backend; do not offer alternative stacks.
The app is a single-user macOS desktop editor for ordinary Markdown files already on disk.
Create the full project, installable with npm install and runnable with npm run tauri dev.
Use a native folder picker, then show a recursive sidebar of only .md and .markdown files.
Create, rename, and delete files inside that chosen folder; require a confirmation before delete and never copy files into an app library.
Use CodeMirror as the authoritative source editor with syntax highlighting, find/replace, undo/redo, and Markdown-aware keyboard shortcuts.
Add a Preview toggle that renders CommonMark plus GFM tables, task lists, fenced code, images, links, and local KaTeX without network requests.
Add a Focus toggle that hides nonessential chrome and centers the document at a readable maximum width.
Autosave with a short debounce through the Rust backend, using atomic writes and a visible saved, saving, or error state.
Watch the active file for external edits and offer Reload or Keep mine rather than silently overwriting either version.
Persist font family, size, line spacing, editor width, syntax visibility, accent color, and light/dark/system appearance locally.
Resolve relative image paths from the document directory and show a clear broken-image state.
If the chosen folder is already a Git repository, show status and explicit Pull and Push buttons that call the user's installed git; display stdout and errors, never auto-commit or auto-push.
Add Open Terminal Here and Copy Folder Path actions, but never embed, launch, or authenticate an AI agent automatically.
Keep the app local-only: no accounts, cloud storage, telemetry, analytics, updater, or credentials.
Deliberately exclude real-time collaboration, mobile clients, OAuth GitHub connection, conflict auto-merging, and a rich Notion-style block editor.
Use accessible labels, logical tab order, visible focus states, and keyboard access for every action.
Add unit tests for path containment, Markdown rendering options, atomic-save failure handling, and Git command parsing.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that opens a fixture folder, edits a file, saves it, and confirms the changed Markdown on disk.
Write a README with prerequisites, setup, permissions, data location, Git behavior, test/build commands, and the deliberate limitations.
Run the tests and production build before finishing; fix failures rather than merely reporting them.
